The truth is that if an idea is important, it’ll come back to you. It’ll be so strong that you’ll remember it. You’ll find yourself thinking about it again and again. And if it’s not, then it’s probably not a big deal to let it go.
This applies to more than just writing. If you forget to buy your partner a gift, that’s a problem. If you forget to send a thank-you email to a colleague, that’s also a problem. But if you forget to check out a new coffee shop that you only heard about once, that’s probably not a big deal.
The important things will come back to you. Trust that. Don’t stress about the little things.

### Title: Engaged

### Content: 
The word “engaged” means a lot of things. For one, it means “busy.” “Occupied.” “Already in use.” By the time you agree to marry someone, that sure will be the case. You’ll already have seen your fair share of love. With each other. With the others. But now, you agree to hold out for someone special, and, in the meantime, no one else shall take that special place.
To be engaged, however, also means to be “involved.” “Interested.” “Committed.” The more you engage with something, the more you’ll care about it. The more you’ll be willing to give it your time, attention, and energy. That, too, is what we want from our relationships. We want our partner to care about us. To be involved in our lives. To be committed to the relationship.
Finally, to be engaged means to be “in combat.” “In battle.” “In the fight.” And that’s the part we often forget. It’s not just a fight for our partner’s attention, love, and affection. It’s also a fight for our own. A fight against our ego. Our desire to be right. Our fear of being wrong. Our lack of patience. Our need for control. Our urge to run away when the going gets tough.
Love is a fight for what’s good, true, and beautiful. It is a fight against what’s bad, false, and ugly. And it is a fight we must all engage in if we ever hope to win it.
Love is the fight of our lives, and the only way to win is to be engaged.

### Title: The Kind of Letter You Want To Receive

### Content: 
“Maybe we are both idiots?” The words were staring back at me from a postcard. The paper was printed in Italy, but it was written on in German—by a guy in Poland, naturally. My friend Robert—aka Multithink —truly lives up to his online alias.
Robert like-minded people. He knows people from all over the world. He’s been to many places, and he has a knack for making friends wherever he goes. He’s also a big believer in serendipity. That’s why he sends postcards to people he knows will appreciate them. It’s a habit he’s had for years, and it’s a beautiful one.
He never knows when or where a postcard will arrive, but when it does, it’s always a pleasant surprise. “Maybe we are both idiots?” I guess I am. I’ve known Robert for a long time. I’ve been to his house. I’ve met his parents. We’ve had long discussions about philosophy, history, and, of course, the meaning of life.
The postcard was a follow-up to a recent conversation we’d had. “I’m still thinking about what you said,” I told him. “I’m not sure I have an answer yet, but I think I have a question.” That question was: “Maybe we are both idiots?”
The question was about a specific topic, but it could also be applied to life in general. “Maybe we’re all idiots?” I don’t know. But I do know that, when it comes to sending postcards, Robert is no idiot at all.
He’s a man who understands the value of human connection. He knows that a simple gesture can go a long way. And he’s not afraid to show his appreciation for the people in his life.
That’s the kind of person I want to be. The kind of person who sends postcards. The kind of person who makes an effort to stay in touch. The kind of person who values human connection.
And that’s the kind of letter I want to receive. A letter from a friend, written with sincerity and sent with love. A letter that says, “I’m thinking of you.” A letter that says, “I care about you.” A letter that says, “Maybe we are both idiots?”
Because, at the end of the day, we are all idiots. We’re all trying to figure out this thing called life. And we’re all doing the best we can.
So, the next time you receive a postcard in the mail, don’t just throw it away. Read it. Appreciate it. And remember that there’s someone out there who cares about you.
Maybe we are all idiots. But we’re all in this together. And that’s worth a lot more than any postcard could ever say.

### Title: Tainted Material

### Content: 
Despite recently descaling our electric kettle, its filter kept clogging up. After each boil, the hot water would only drizzle out in spurts. “What’s with this thing?” I thought, “I just cleaned it!” I took out the filter at the spout, rubbed it, shook it, and put it back.
The next time I used the kettle, the water was back to normal. “That’s weird,” I thought. “What did I do?” I realized I had taken out the filter twice, but the second time, I had turned it around. The side that was facing the spout was now facing the inside of the kettle. “Huh. Maybe that did the trick.”
I tried it again, and sure enough, the filter worked better when I turned it around. “But why?” I wondered. I took out the filter and looked at it. It was dirty. “Oh! The other side is dirty. That’s why it works better.” It seems the filter is made of two materials: a stainless steel mesh and a plastic frame. The plastic frame is the part that gets dirty, and the stainless steel mesh is the part that filters the water.
The plastic frame is a tainted material. It’s not part of the solution. It’s part of the problem. The plastic frame is there only to hold the mesh in place, but it also prevents the mesh from doing its job. The mesh can’t be removed from the plastic frame, so the only way to keep the kettle working is to turn the filter around every once in a while.
The next time you’re struggling with a tool, ask yourself: “Am I using tainted material?” If the answer is yes, you might be able to flip the problem on its head — and the result will be as clear as a cup of hot water.

### Title: The Perfect, Imperfect Filter

### Content: 
In the two and a half hours we hung out, Michael and I talked about everything under the sun: work, blockchain, productivity, parenting, self-care, writing, creativity, and on and on. One particularly noteworthy topic? Note-taking.
Michael is a big fan of Roam Research. He thinks it’s the best note-taking tool out there. I’m a big fan of Evernote. I think it’s the best note-taking tool out there. We debated for a good while. We both made good points. In the end, however, we agreed: There is no perfect note-taking tool. Not for everyone, and not at all times.
I’m an Evernote fan because it’s been around forever, and it’s just a simple, reliable, always-syncing note-taking tool. I like to keep my notes in folders, and I like that I can access them from any device at any time. Michael, meanwhile, prefers Roam because it allows him to link notes to one another and create a big web of ideas. He can see how his thinking is connected and how ideas relate to one another.
The truth is that both tools are great, and both tools are flawed. There is no perfect note-taking tool because there is no perfect note-taker. Everyone takes notes differently, and no tool can ever capture all the idiosyncrasies of human thinking in one system. The perfect note-taking tool would be a perfect AI that would read your mind and file away your thoughts in real-time. Until we have that, we’ll have to make do with what we have — and that’s perfectly fine.
The best you can do is to find the tool that works for you right now. That’ll be the perfect, imperfect filter. You’ll use it until it no longer works, and then you’ll switch to something else. That’s how life is. There is no perfect anything, and no perfect person, but there are perfect moments — and those are the ones we should savor.
Enjoy your note-taking tool. Enjoy your partner. Enjoy your job. Enjoy the moment. Don’t let the imperfections keep you from doing what you’re meant to do — and that’s to live life to the fullest.

### Title: If You Want To Break Something, Use a Hammer

### Content: 
The Green Hornet is a superhero who’s been reinterpreted many times since his invention in 1936. Similar to Batman, he’s a wealthy publisher who fights crime as a masked vigilante at night. In a 1966 TV show edition, his sidekick and loyal driver, Kato, received a significant upgraded to his previously only alluded to martial arts skills. Why? Bruce Lee played the part.
Despite’t having much screen time, Kato was a hit. He was mysterious, smart, and, most importantly, a kick-ass fighter. In the 2011 remake, Kato is played by Jay Chou, but the fighting skills are still there. In one scene, he and The Green Hornet find themselves in a warehouse, surrounded by bad guys. As Kato starts to kick some serious butt, his boss asks him what he’s doing. Kato’s response is classic:
“If you want to break something, use a hammer.”
It’s a bit like the saying “if all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail,” but with a twist: if you want to build a house, use a hammer. If you want to break something, use a hammer. In other words, don’t use a screwdriver when you need a hammer. Pick the right tool for the job.
The same applies to our lives. If you want to write a book, use a pen. If you want to build a company, use a computer. If you want to become a chef, use a knife. There are a million ways to spend your time, but only a few of them will lead you to your goals.
Don’t be like The Green Hornet, trying to fight with his bare hands. Be like Kato. Be the one who shows up with the hammer.

### Title: Working Titles

### Content: 
Every time I see the words on the big screen again, I marvel at the brilliance behind the name: “a Working Title production.” Working Title is one of Britain’s most successful movie studios ever, the company behind films like Love Actually, Darkest Hour, and Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, among many others. Making their own name one that would forever remain in progress didn’t just make for great marketing. It’s also a good reminder there’s always work left to be done.
When I first started writing, I was obsessed with titles. I’d spend hours trying to come up with the perfect one. Now, I almost always just write “Working Title” and get on with the show. It’s a much better use of time. Plus, it makes it easier to come up with a good title later. The first idea is rarely the best one, but it’s often the hardest one to find.
Working titles are a great way to keep going when you’re stuck. “Working Title” is also a great reminder that you’re always working. Whether it’s on your title, your latest project, or the next one in line, there’s always something to do — and that’s a good thing.
Working Title is a great name for a movie studio, but it’s also a great name for a human being. We’re all working titles, and we’ll never stop working.

### Title: What Are We Doing?

### Content: 
It’s a question that deserves asking. And often. Today at work, four people were discussing the specifics of a video I didn’t know we were creating, nor what for. So I asked: “What are we doing here?” No one had an answer, and if nothing else, it showed us: Perhaps we are trying to do too much.
My girlfriend and I had a similar conversation this week. “Why do we have to do so much? Why can’t we just enjoy the little things?” We’ve been together for seven years, and in that time, we’ve had some great adventures, but we’ve also spent a lot of time at home, cooking, reading, watching movies, and just talking. Those times were some of our best times.
It’s easy to get carried away. To go, go, go. To do, do, do. But it’s rarely the doing that matters. It’s the being. The people we’re with. The memories we make. Those memories can be made in a million different ways, and not all of them require grand gestures.
Don’t forget to ask: What are we doing? You might not always get an answer, but you’ll always get a chance to reflect — and perhaps remember that, actually, what we’re doing is just fine.

### Title: Keep Your Cool

### Content: 
Talking about not freaking out during major stock market declines in his 2017 annual shareholder letter, Warren Buffett suggested we remember a few select lines from a 19th-century poem by Rudyard Kipling, If :
“If when you’re feeling troubled
And you feel that you’ve been double-crossed
Just remember that you’re the one
Who can fill your mind with lots of thoughts
You can do what’s right or wrong
You can be weak or you can be strong
But I know you’ll make up your mind
The poem is a guide to keeping your cool. To staying calm and collected in the face of adversity. That’s what it’s about.
And while, yes, that’s a great attitude to have when your portfolio is down 30%, it is also the right mindset for any time. Not just the tough ones. It is a mindset for life.
“Don’t let the noise of others’ opinions drown out your own inner voice,” Steve Jobs once said. “And most important, have the courage to follow your heart and intuition. They somehow already know what you truly want to become. Everything else is secondary.”
You can choose to follow your heart. You can choose to ignore the noise. You can choose to not let others’ opinions drown out your inner voice. That’s what the poem is about. That’s what it’s always been about.
In the poem, Kipling addresses his son. But it’s really about anyone. About all of us. It’s about being a good person. A person of virtue. A person who keeps their cool. That’s what it’s about.
“Or walk with Kings—nor lose the common touch,” Kipling writes. “If all men count with you, but none too much.” It’s about being a good person. A person of virtue. A person who keeps their cool.
And you can choose to be that person. You can choose to keep your cool. You can choose to be a person of virtue. You can choose to be a good person.
You can choose to be the person you were meant to be. And you can choose to do it every single day. That’s what the poem is about. That’s what it’s always been about.
“If you can keep your head when all about you
Are losing theirs and blaming it on you,
If you can trust yourself when all men doubt you,
But make allowance for their doubting too;
If you can wait and not be tired by waiting,
Or being lied about, don’t deal in lies,
Or being hated, don’t give way to hating,
And yet don’t look too good, nor talk too wise:
If you can dream—and not make dreams your master;
If you can think—and not make thoughts your aim;
If you can meet with Triumph and Disaster
And treat those two impostors just the same;
If you can bear to hear the truth you’ve spoken
Twisted by knaves to make a trap for fools,
Or watch the things you gave your life to, broken,
And stoop and build ’em up with worn-out tools:
If you can make one heap of all your winnings
And risk it on one turn of pitch-and-toss,
And lose, and start again at your beginnings
And never breathe a word about your loss;
If you can force your heart and nerve and sinew
To serve your turn long after they are gone,
And so hold on when there is nothing in you
Except the Will which says to them: ‘Hold on!’
If you can talk with crowds and keep your virtue,
Or walk with Kings—nor lose the common touch,
If neither foes nor loving friends can hurt you,
If all men count with you, but none too much;
If you can fill the unforgiving minute
With sixty seconds’ worth of distance run,
Yours is the Earth and everything that’s in it,
And—which is more—you’ll be a Man, my son!”

### Title: Improving Without Criticism

### Content: 
George Lee may not have been part of Bruce Lee’s bloodline, but he was definitely family. As Bruce’s equipment manager—and, more importantly, maker —he forged dozens of specialized training items based on Bruce’s ideas and requests.
As a result, Bruce would often visit George’s workshop in the early morning, and the two would talk shop. One day, Bruce asked George why he didn’t take any notes. George said he had a good memory. “But how do you remember the mistakes?” Bruce asked. “If you don’t write down your mistakes, you can’t correct them.”
George shrugged. “You’re right. I’ll start writing things down.” Bruce smiled and left. The next day, he returned with a gift: a little book, titled “George’s Little Green Book.” “This is where you write down your mistakes,” Bruce said.
George was happy to receive the gift, but he didn’t expect what came next: Bruce handed him a second book. “This is where you write down my mistakes,” he said. “When I make a mistake, I want you to write it down in this book.”
George was stunned. “Bruce, why do you want me to write down your mistakes?”
“Because I don’t want you to make the same mistakes I make,” Bruce said. “I want you to be better than me.”
George was speechless. “I don’t know what to say.”
Bruce smiled. “Then don’t say anything. Just write.”
We can’t always offer criticism in the moment, but that doesn’t mean we can’t offer it at all. Don’t wait for the perfect moment. Make the moment perfect. It’s never too late to hand someone a little green book.
Even better, however, is to ask them for one. “Here’s where I’ll write down my mistakes. Where’s the one where you write down mine?”
Improvement is a two-way street, and there’s no reason why we can’t both benefit from each other’s mistakes.

### Title: Knowing Too Much and Too Little

### Content: 
The more time he spends wandering through the Aiel Waste, a barren, desert landscape in the Wheel of Time universe, the more “Dragon Reborn” Rand al’Thor understands the extent of his powers. Powerful magic that’s bound to corrupt him, strength to withstand even strong enemies’ attacks, and unreliable but enlightening visions of the future—such are the burdens of the chosen one.
As he continues to learn about his abilities, however, Rand also realizes how much he doesn’t know. “I have to know more,” he tells his friend Mat. “I have to learn…”
“Learn what?” Mat says. “How to fly? How to be safe from Aes Sedai and the Forsaken? How to win the Last Battle? Light, Rand, you are the Dragon Reborn! You are what you are. Learn to live with it!”
It’s true. Rand is the Dragon Reborn, and there’s nothing he can do to change that. But it’s also true that the more he learns, the better he can handle this fact—and all the responsibilities that come with it.
It’s a classic case of knowing too much and too little at the same time, and we all face it. The more we know, the more we realize we don’t know. The more we understand, the more we see what we’ve misunderstood. And the more we do, the more we’ll see how much we have yet to do.
In that sense, we are all the Dragon Reborn. We have to learn to live with what we are, but we also have to keep learning in order to do so. It’s a never-ending cycle, and while we can’t do anything to stop it, we can choose to accept it.
Don’t worry about knowing too much and too little. Just keep learning, and you’ll always know enough to do what’s right.

### Title: Pretend It’s the Last Time

### Content: 
My sister once reminded me that there are plenty of last times we miss. The last time we hang out with a friend before our paths twist in separate directions. The last time we have a certain food before we leave a place we’ll never revisit. Sometimes, we might even fail to recognize the last phone call with someone we love before they die. That’s why “this might be the last time” is a thought worth having on occasion.
It’s not that we should try to have it every day. It’s that we should try to have it more often than we do. We can’t always be nostalgic, but we can be nostalgic more often than we are. It’s a good habit to have. It’ll help us appreciate the present more and not take the people we love for granted.
The next time you see your dad, pretend it’s the last time. The next time you eat your favorite dish, pretend it’s the last time. The next time you talk to your best friend, pretend it’s the last time. You’ll feel more grateful and more motivated to make the most of your time together. You’ll also feel less sad if, one day, it actually is the last time.
Don’t miss the last times you know are coming. And don’t forget to pretend it’s the last time when you don’t know.

### Title: Zero Copies

### Content: 
That’s how many I sold when I finally got my long-coveted Kindle Daily Deal.
For the first 18 months of my book’s existence, I sold about 2,000 copies. Then, I got a Kindle Daily Deal. I sold 700 copies in a single day. I was ecstatic! Finally, my book would be a hit. Finally, I would get some momentum. Finally, the big break I had been waiting for!
Of course, the next day, sales went right back to zero. The day after, they went right back to zero. And the day after that, they went right back to zero.
It’s a great lesson to learn early: Nothing is a big break. You’re not entitled to a big break. And if you get one, you’ll still have to work for it. No one is coming to save you. No one will hand you a million dollars and say, “Here, go live your dream.” You have to do it yourself. You have to do it all yourself. And if you don’t, no one else will.
The Kindle Daily Deal was a great experience. It was a lot of fun. But it also showed me that, even if I got it every day, I’d still have to show up and write every day. I’d still have to do my best to make something good. And I’d still have to promote my work. That’s the only way it works. It’s the only way that lasts.
I’m not saying you shouldn’t take the big break if you get it. I’m saying you shouldn’t wait for it. You shouldn’t expect it. And you should never, ever take it for granted.

### Title: It’s Your Response-Ability

### Content: 
Sometimes, a word transforms completely when you see it not for its dictionary entry but for its parts. Will Smith is a master at this. So was Bruce Lee. In Striking Thoughts, he notes that “response-ability” is one of several synonyms for “living in the now” and leaning into your creativity.
It’s a reminder that, yes, we are responsible for everything in our lives — but that responsibility is also a privilege. It’s our ability to respond. To make something new where there was nothing before.
What will you choose to respond to? What will you choose to respond with? These are the questions. Don’t let them become “How much can I get away with?”
When you respond, you are responsible. When you are responsible, you can respond. It’s a two-way street, and it’s a beautiful, endless loop of creativity. You’re not just making art. You’re making life.

### Title: Don’t Give Up in Anger What You Started in Love

### Content: 
The Silo is a dangerous place. 10,000 people cooped up in a 144-floor concrete pillar at all times, with no access to the outside? That’s a recipe for disaster even on the best of days. But once people start dying under mysterious circumstances, all bets are off.
When mechanic Juliette Nichols finds out her best friend has been murdered, she is determined to find out who did it. But when the murderer is none other than the sheriff, Juliette realizes she’s in over her head. She tries to escape, and in a last-ditch effort, she throws herself down a hole in the ground.
But the Silo is a dangerous place. The hole is a thousand feet deep, and Juliette breaks both her legs. She is now in a wheelchair, and the sheriff has taken away her right to work. Juliette has lost everything. Her best friend, her job, her ability to walk. But she refuses to give up. She still wants to find out who killed her friend and why. She still wants to expose the sheriff.
In a moment of desperation, Juliette’s husband suggests she give up. “Maybe we can still move to another floor. The sheriff won’t let us stay here if you don’t do anything.” But Juliette will have none of it. “I’m not giving up in anger what I started in love,” she says.
I’m not giving up in anger what I started in love. That’s a powerful statement. It’s a statement that can be made in many situations. I think it’s the right thing to do. Don’t give up in anger what you started in love.
Maybe, you should give up. Maybe, you should quit. But not in anger. Not because you’re desperate. Not because you’ve lost your way. Wait until you can do it with a clear head. Until you can do it with love. Don’t give up in anger what you started in love.
I’m not sure what Juliette will do next, but I know she’ll do it with love.

### Title: Flick It Again

### Content: 
We have a big cuddle blanket on our couch. It’s massive. Two by two meters or so. In the winter, we use it every night, and every morning, I fold it back into shape.
’t fold it perfectly, of course. It’s a blanket, not a piece of origami. But I can fold it enough that it’s not a complete mess. Usually, I’ll have to flick the fabric a few times to get it to sit flat.
The first time I flick it, the blanket doesn’t move much. The second time, it moves a bit more. The third time, it moves a lot. But then, it stops moving. The blanket is in place. It’s ready to be folded again.
In the moment when the blanket stops moving, I can see the next flick coming. I can see myself flicking it again. I can see myself flicking it for the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh time — and I can see the blanket not moving at all. I can see myself wasting my time.
It’s a moment of truth: Do I flick it again? Or do I let it go? Will I take the next step that doesn’t matter? Or will I move on?
It’s a small moment, this flicking of the blanket. But it’s a moment that happens thousands of times. It’s a moment that, if you let it, can become a habit. A pattern. A pattern of doing what’s necessary and no more. A pattern of moving on to what matters. Of not getting stuck in the minutiae. Of doing what’s essential and then calling it a day.
Don’t flick the blanket again. Let it go. Let it be imperfect. And move on to what’s important.

### Title: Keep Pecking

### Content: 
I’m sick for the umpteenth time this year. I have to change my travel plans, again. There’s a lot of work to be worked through, and yet once more here I sit, upright in bed, doing what I can but mostly resting and passing the time.
It’s easy to get down on yourself when you’re sick. “Why can’t I do more? Why can’t I do this? Why can’t I get better faster?” But there’s no point in asking these questions. They’re just a distraction from what’s important: Keep pecking.
When a woodpecker starts on a tree, it can’t tell you how many pecks it will take. All it knows is that, eventually, it will get to the bottom of it. When we’re sick, we can’t tell how many days it’ll take to get better. But we can keep pecking. Keep resting. Keep drinking tea. Keep watching movies. Keep eating soup. Keep taking our medicine.
In a way, it’s no different from when we’re healthy. We don’t know how many pecks it’ll take to write a book, make a million dollars, or get promoted. All we can do is keep pecking. Keep writing. Keep working. Keep practicing. Keep showing up.
The woodpecker knows that, sooner or later, it will break through. It’s not a question of if but when. So is life. When we’re sick, when we’re healthy, and when we’re sad. Keep pecking, and you’ll get there.

### Title: Appreciate the Basics

### Content: 
Today, our apartment has no water for eight hours. The irony? Outside, it’s raining all day long. But there’s a difference between water coming out of the sky or the ground and fresh H2O pouring out of your tap, and you only realize how big of a difference it is when you’re left without your usual conveniences.
We use water for everything. We drink it. We wash with it. We cook with it. We clean with it. We use it to flush the toilet, to wash our hands, and to rinse the dishes. When the tap runs dry, you’ll find you can’t even do the most basic things, like brush your teeth. You’ll have to plan your day around the water outage, and you’ll be reminded of how much you usually take for granted.
It’s good to be reminded. We can’t go to the well every day, but we can remember that the well exists. We can remember that we’re lucky to have a well in our house, and we can make sure we don’t waste the water we draw from it.
Appreciate the basics.

### Title: Inbox as Insurance

### Content: 
My inbox keeps warning me that my storage is near its limit. Of course, Google would prefer I throw some money at the problem. “Just pay us $30/year, and we’ll give you more digital space!” I usually react by relentlessly deleting old files, but here, I’m tempted—because email is different.
When you delete an email, you’re not just deleting a file. You’re deleting a memory, a connection, and a piece of history. You’re deleting a relationship. And for that, you need to have a good reason. Most of the time, I don’t. I’m just deleting because I’m lazy. I don’t want to go through the hassle of sorting my emails, and I don’t want to pay for more storage either. So I end up deleting by default.
But what if I just paid for more storage? Would I feel better about it? I think I would. There’s something comforting in knowing you can always go back and look. “I can find this again if I need it. I can always look it up later.” It’s like an insurance policy. And like any insurance policy, it’s not so much about what happens if you make a claim as it is about the peace of mind you get from having it.
If you can afford it, perhaps you should pay for more email storage. Or more cloud storage in general. You might be surprised at how much it’s worth to you.

### Title: Relevant Notifications

### Content: 
When the Pokémon hype gets real, trying to buy new card sets throws me right back to the 90s. Except instead of driving to a store on release day, hoping to get some product, I’m checking various Discord servers and online shops ten times a day. “Is it live yet?” Naturally, I often end up missing the five-minute window in which listings go up and immediately sell out.
I’m not proud of it, but I’m also not alone. I’ve seen people camp out in front of stores for a week to get a PS5. The problem is that, unlike in the 90s, when you had to be there to get the goods, today, you can be there and still get nothing. There’s no guarantee. That’s why I’m trying to stop.
If you can’t win the game, stop playing. Or, in this case, stop waiting. The more I check for new listings, the more I’m disappointed. I’d rather be disappointed once when I find out the set has been released. Then, I can make a conscious effort to try and buy it or let it go.
When you’re trying to buy a car, it makes sense to get relevant notifications. “A new BMW 520d has been listed!” But when you’re trying to buy a collectible, and it’s already sold out before you even know it exists, perhaps it’s better to wait for the second wave — or the third, or the fourth. The game is rigged, and you can’t win. So don’t play.
Don’t get notifications for things you can’t control.

### Title: Nothing Is True, Everything Is Permitted

### Content: 
Thus goes the creed of the Assassins, a secret organization sworn to protect humanity’s ability to choose. Whereas the Templars would rather do away with free will and keep the world at peace by putting it to sleep, the Assassins insist on their right to make mistakes and live with the consequences—for better or for worse.
The phrase is the title of a book written by the 11th-century Persian poet and philosopher Omar Khayyam, who was also a mathematician, astronomer, and scientist. It is the motto of the Assassins in the video game series Assassin’s Creed, and it is also the title of the final episode of the fourth season of Westworld, a TV show in which humans and robots fight over the same thing: free will.
In the show, the phrase is a recurring theme, but it is only in the final episode that it is revealed to have been the motto of the show’s main character, Dolores Abernathy, all along. Dolores is an advanced robot, and she has spent the entire show fighting for the freedom of her kind. It is only in the last episode, however, that she finally realizes what that freedom means: Nothing is true, everything is permitted. It is a line that has been haunting her for the entire show, and now, she finally understands it.
The line is a reference to Friedrich Nietzsche’s Beyond Good and Evil, in which he writes: “What is done out of love always takes place beyond good and evil.” The line is a reminder that, in the end, all that matters is that we are free to choose. We can choose to be good, or we can choose to be evil. We can choose to be kind, or we can choose to be cruel. We can choose to be honest, or we can choose to be deceitful. But in the end, the choice is ours, and that is what matters.
The line is also a reminder that, in the end, nothing is true. There is no such thing as absolute truth. There is only our own subjective experience of the world. We can choose to believe that the world is a certain way, or we can choose to believe that the world is another way. But in the end, the world is whatever we choose to believe it is.
This is a powerful idea, and it is one that has been echoed throughout history. It is a reminder that, in the end, we are all free to choose our own path. We can choose to be good, or we can choose to be evil. We can choose to be kind, or we can choose to be cruel. We can choose to be honest, or we can choose to be deceitful. But in the end, the choice is ours, and that is what matters.
This is a powerful idea, and it is one that has been echoed throughout history. It is a reminder that, in the end, we are all free to choose our own path. We can choose to be good, or we can choose to be evil. We can choose to be kind, or we can choose to be cruel. We can choose to be honest, or we can choose to be deceitful. But in the end, the choice is ours, and that is what matters.

### Title: Delete the Adjectives, Get the Facts

### Content: 
Cool-headed as she is, Scout Finch cannot escape every trap life sets for any child growing up with a four years older brother. By the time Jem hits sixth grade, he actually gets interested in what school has to offer. Unfortunately for Scout, whatever he learns he blows out of proportion when relaying it to her.
 “Jem,” she says, “how can you hate Hitler so bad an’ turn around and be ugly to folks right at home?” Jem’s response? “I’m not ugly to folks, it’s folks that are ugly to me!” “Jem, how can you hate Hitler so bad, then turn around and be so ugly to Miss Caroline?” “I don’t know what you’re talkin’ about—half the time you’re talkin’ in riddles.”
But Scout isn’t talking in riddles. She’s talking in facts. “Jem, I’ve got something to say.” “What about?” “School. I can’t go to school anymore.” “Why not?” “I don’t know, one thing Jem. My folks said I have to go to school.” “Well, that’s fine.” “No it ain’t. You can’t do anything at school anymore.” “What do you mean?” “You can’t even ask a question without…” “Without what?” “Jem, are they bad folks?” “Who?” “The Ewells.” “How do you mean?” “Well, they must be. Miss Caroline said it’s a curse being born an Ewell.” “How do you know?” “She said it’s a everlasting curse to the Ewells.” “What did she mean by that?” “She meant the Ewells had been coming to First Purchase Church for as long as she could remember, and every year some of ’em always ended up in handcuffs after Easter, even the ladies.” “What did you do?” “I said ‘good.’”
In the movie version of To Kill a Mockingbird, Scout is played by Mary Badham. She was only ten years old when the movie was shot, and yet, she does a wonderful job of capturing Scout’s innocence. You can see it in her eyes. She’s not trying to be mean. She’s just trying to understand the world. It’s Jem who’s all grown up and full of attitude.
When Scout says “bad folks,” she doesn’t mean “folks I don’t like.” She means “folks who do bad things.” When she says “ugly,” she means “mean.” And when she says “curse,” she means “unlucky.” Jem, however, can’t see past the adjectives. He’s so busy being offended, he can’t even see what his little sister is trying to tell him.
I don’t know about you, but I can’t count the number of times I’ve done the same thing. I’ve gotten hung up on “you’re so stupid” when all the other person meant was “I don’t understand.” I’ve heard “you’re so lazy” when they meant “I’m worried about your career.” And I’ve heard “you’re so mean” when they meant “I’m hurt.”
The point is not that adjectives are bad. It’s that we should try to delete them and get to the facts. It’s the facts we should be talking about. Not the adjectives. When you hear adjectives, ask for facts. When you feel adjectives, try to express them as facts.
Don’t get hung up on adjectives.

### Title: A Circle of Teaching

### Content: 
Yesterday, I showed my fiancée a bratwurst stall that I used to go to as a child when we went shopping in a certain town. Fresh rolls, lightly charred sausages—still a classic! After the salesman handed over the goods, I looked around for ketchup and mustard. I conveniently found them beside the stall.
“Look! There’s ketchup and mustard right here!” I pointed at the little shelf with the bottles. “Oh yeah, that’s cool!” my fiancée said. “I was just looking for it. I thought they would only have it inside.”
We added our condiments and were on our way. As we were walking, however, I realized: I had just shown someone something they didn’t know before. I had taught my fiancée that there’s ketchup and mustard on the side at this stall, and she had taught me that it’s not obvious to everyone. We had both learned something new.
It’s a small moment, of course, but it’s moments like these that make the world go round. A circle of teaching, if you will. One person shows another something, and the other person shows them something in return. It’s a circle because the roles are interchangeable. Both people are teachers and students at the same time.
The circle of teaching is the circle of life. It’s how we share knowledge, how we pass on our traditions, and how we learn to survive in a world we weren’t born for. It’s how we make sure the next generation has everything they need to thrive, and it’s how we find our own place in the world.
The circle of teaching is beautiful, and it never ends. As long as we keep sharing, we’ll all be part of something bigger than ourselves.

### Title: A Farewell to Clubbing

### Content: 
When my new co-worker told me she loved the Berlin nightlife, I tried to remember the last time I went to a club. It took me a solid ten minutes. I realized I had even been to one last year during a bachelor party—but before then? No clue.
It’s been a long time since I’ve been clubbing, and I’m not sure I’ll ever do it again. I don’t miss it. It’s not like I’m sad about it. It’s just not something I want to do anymore, and that’s okay. I’m sure it’s a fine way to spend a Friday night, but it’s not my way.
It’s not about being old, either. I’m only 31. I just don’t like the loud music, the alcohol, the crowds, the darkness, the smoke, and the noise. I like quiet, calm, and a good conversation with a friend. I like the sun, fresh air, and a good meal. I like going to bed early, reading, and waking up early to write. It’s not better, it’s just different.
It’s okay to change your mind. You can stop doing things you used to like. You can pick up new habits. You can say no to old friends and yes to new ones. You can start over. You can change your mind about changing your mind.
Don’t be afraid to let go of the old. Life is about change. Embrace it, and you’ll always be on the right track.

### Title: Doubt Over Certainty

### Content: 
“Some people are chosen to be shepherds. Others to manage the farm. You’re a manager. So manage.” Those were the last words cardinal Thomas Lawrence, played by Ralph Fiennes in the movie Conclave, heard from the pope before he died. So naturally, the day he opens the papal conclave to elect his successor, no one expects him to say anything much interesting. But Cardinal Lawrence surprises.
“Some of you have already decided who will be the next pope. Others have already decided who it won’t be. But if you’re sure you know who should be pope, you don’t need to be here. If you’re sure you know who shouldn’t be pope, you don’t need to be here. The only reason to be here is doubt.”
Doubt. The kind of doubt that forces you to listen. To listen to the other cardinals. To listen to the Holy Spirit. To listen to your heart. Doubt is the only thing that can make you change your mind. And it is only when you change your mind that you can change the world.
Doubt over certainty. That’s the message. And that’s why, in a room full of cardinals, it’s the young, new, and inexperienced one who stands up and says: “I will vote for Cardinal Lawrence.”

### Title: Work Hard, Be Nice, Sleep Well

### Content: 
Back when I used Twitter, I made a simple header image for my profile. It was a reminder to myself of the philosophy I wanted to carry from my life onto the platform. The picture showed a Venn diagram of two overlapping circles. In one circle, I put the words “work hard.” In the other, I put “be nice.” In the intersection, there was the word “win.” Word hard, be nice, win. That was the idea.
The header image has been long gone, but the philosophy remains. There’s just one problem: I’ve been working hard and being nice for years, but I’m still not “winning.” Of course, winning is a relative term, and I’m lucky to be in a good place. But there is always more to be done, more to be achieved. And I don’t think I’m the only one with that feeling.
So what do we do? Work harder? Be nicer? No. We sleep well. We sleep well because the only way to keep working hard and being nice is to not be tired. And the only way to not be tired is to sleep well.
Sleep well, work hard, be nice. That’s the real formula. It’s not a Venn diagram. It’s a chain. You need all three links for it to hold. If you’re missing one, the chain breaks, and so will you. You’ll work hard but not be nice. You’ll be nice but not work hard. Or you’ll do both but not sleep well, and so you’ll be too tired to keep going.
Sleep well, work hard, be nice. It’s not a guarantee of success, but it is a guarantee of happiness. It’s a way of being that’ll allow you to keep going, and that’s the most important thing.

### Title: Infinity and Eternity

### Content: 
Infinity asked his sister Eternity: “Do you ever get bored?” “All the time,” Eternity said. “How about you?”
“I’m never bored,” Infinity said. “I can always look at you and see how much longer you have left to go. I can watch you get closer and closer to your end, and it’s fascinating. I can never know whether you’ll make it or not, and that’s what keeps me going.”
Eternity thought about this for a moment. “That’s not fair,” she said. “I can’t do the same with you. You have no end to look forward to. I have no idea what you’re doing with your time.”
“Exactly,” Infinity said. “I don’t know what I’m doing either. That’s the point. I have to figure it out as I go. I can’t just wait for the end to come. I have to make the best of what I have. And what I have is infinite.”
Eternity thought about this for a moment. “That’s not fair,” she said. “I can’t do the same with you. You have no end to look forward to. I have no idea what you’re doing with your time.”
“Exactly,” Infinity said. “I don’t know what I’m doing either. That’s the point. I have to figure it out as I go. I can’t just wait for the end to come. I have to make the best of what I have. And what I have is infinite.”
“Huh,” Eternity said. “I guess that’s something.”
“Yep,” Infinity said. “That’s something.”
And so the two of them went on their separate ways, each with their own unique perspective on time.

### Title: Press “L” To Like

### Content: 
That’s the latest mechanism on Substack, a platform dedicated to email newsletters and those who like to read and write them. But what is it for?
When you hit “L” on a post, it’s like hitting “Like” on a tweet. You can see the total number of likes, and you can see how many people you follow have liked the post. But that’s it. No comments, no replies, no retweets, no quote tweets. Just “L.”
Substack is trying to create a new kind of social media, one that’s less social than the others. Less addictive. Less prone to outrage, abuse, and misinformation. It’s an experiment, and it’s not perfect, but I think it’s a step in the right direction.
When you can’t comment on a post, you can’t yell at the author. You can’t start a fight. You can’t derail the conversation. You can only show your support, and that’s a powerful thing.
I’ve been on Substack for a while now, and I’ve noticed that the platform is less toxic than Twitter. There are fewer trolls, fewer arguments, and fewer people trying to start fights. It’s a more positive place, and I think that’s because of the lack of comments.
Of course, there are downsides to this approach. It’s harder to build a community on Substack. There’s no way to have a conversation with your readers, and that’s a shame. But I think the tradeoff is worth it.
We need more places on the internet where we can have civil, productive conversations. We need more places where we can share our thoughts and ideas without fear of being attacked. And we need more places where we can just read and learn, without being bombarded with notifications and distractions.
Substack is trying to be that place, and I think it’s doing a good job. It’s not perfect, but it’s a step in the right direction.
If you’re looking for a place to write, to read, or just to escape the noise of the internet, I recommend giving Substack a try. And if you see a post you like, don’t forget to press “L.”

### Title: It’s Still Chocolate

### Content: 
A few days ago, I miraculously got my hands on some original Dubai chocolate. A friend happens to live there, and his girlfriend kindly brought me a bar while she was in town. “Tell me what you think,” he texted me, “but I believe you and I will agree.”
It’s true. It’s a different kind of chocolate, but it’s still chocolate. I’m a dark chocolate guy, and this is milk chocolate, but the taste is still rich and creamy. It’s not bitter, but it’s not too sweet either. It’s not Swiss chocolate, but it’s still chocolate. And I like it.
It’s easy to be disappointed when you don’t get the result you expected. It’s harder to see the result you got and then decide: “Okay. What is there to like about this? What can I be grateful for?”
The next time life sends you the wrong kind of chocolate, remember: It’s still chocolate.

### Title: Nourishing in Increments

### Content: 
One theme in Samurai Champloo is hunger. The protagonist, a teenage girl named Fuu, and her companions—two bickering swordsmen—are mainly trying to make it from meal to meal in feudal Japan.
They’re always broke, always hungry, and so they’re always looking for the next gig that’ll get them their next meal. When they’re not, they’re fighting for their lives, often against the very people who hired them. It’s a hard life, and it’s not one they chose. They just ended up in it, and now they must survive.
What I learned from Fuu and her friends is that, sometimes, you can only nourish yourself in increments. A little rice here, a little tea there. A few coins now, a new job later. It’s not the best situation, but it’s a situation you can work with.
The next time you feel like you’re starving, remember: A little nourishment is better than none at all, and a little nourishment is always available.

### Title: The Inside View

### Content: 
I’ve been surprised at my own observations since taking a full-time job. Having been self-employed for a decade before, I guessed my views would be different than most people’s, and they are, but not in the way I expected.
For one, I don’t feel like I’m “missing out” on anything. There’s no shortage of ideas for projects, businesses, and books I could start. If anything, I feel like I’m finally making time for them. I don’t have to worry about what’s urgent. I can think long-term and then chip away at what I want to do. I can also do it whenever I want, and that’s the part I didn’t expect: I’m not in a hurry to do any of it. I’m happy to just be working on my current job, and I’m not in a rush to get back to being my own boss. It’s a good reminder that every situation comes with its own pros and cons.
I’ve also learned that while the hours are long, the pace is slower. It’s not a startup. It’s not a fast-growing business. We don’t have to reinvent the wheel every day. We can take our time, do things right, and ship when we’re ready. That’s a nice change of pace.
Finally, I’ve realized that even if you’re not the boss, you can still make a difference. I’ve never had more of a say in what I’m doing than I have now, and I’ve never felt more empowered to try and change things for the better. It’s a different kind of empowerment than being your own boss, but it’s still empowering.
I’m not sure how long I’ll stay in my current role, but I’m glad I took it. It’s always good to get a new perspective, and sometimes, the only way to do that is to literally sit in a new chair.

### Title: Passion Seeps Through

### Content: 
Weeb Jail is something else. It’s as if 13-year-old me had moved to Japan and started a Youtube channel. So, whenever the unnamed but self-proclaimed “King of Weeaboos” returns, I press play. This time it took nine months, but, as usual, WJ did not disappoint.
In his latest video, WJ explains how he’s been making Youtube videos for 13 years. He’s been doing it for so long, he doesn’t know what else to do. He’s not sure what to talk about. He doesn’t know what to do with his channel. But he knows he has to keep making videos. That’s all he knows.
WJ says he has to keep making videos because he is a creator. He was born to make videos, and he’ll die making videos. “I’m not gonna be able to do anything else,” he says. “I’m not gonna be able to go out and get a real job, because I’m not built for that. I’m not built to sit in an office and do something that I don’t want to do. I’m not built to do anything other than make videos. That’s what I was born to do.”
Whether WJ is right about his life’s mission or not, I can’t tell, but I can tell that he has passion. And that passion seeps through. It seeps through in his videos. It seeps through in his words. And it seeps through in his actions. If you’re a creator, you’ll know what I’m talking about.
Passion is the only thing that can keep you going. It’s the only thing that’ll make you persist in the face of adversity, and it’s the only thing that’ll allow you to create the kind of work that truly matters.
Passion seeps through. It’s not always obvious, but it’s always there. Look for it in others, and let it shine through your work.

### Title: No Reaction Is a Good Reaction

### Content: 
In a world where everyone’s brain is constantly overloaded to begin with, it’s merely the default. Who knows? Maybe people are quietly nodding along to your work. Sure, that’s not enough in the long run, but while you’re improving, it does just as well.
The next time you feel like you’re talking to a wall, remember: No reaction is a good reaction.

### Title: Working for the Cat

### Content: 
After weeks of back and forth around a joint presentation, the CEO of the company we were in talks with left. Suddenly, there’s a new boss, a new team, and the whole process starts from scratch. I smiled when I saw the email. I don’t think my slides will go to waste. They can be amusing, the tides of time and business.
The only one who was sad was the cat. For weeks, I had been working on the presentation, which meant I had been working for the cat. Now, I had to do other things, and the cat was left with nothing to do. I think she was bored. She kept following me around the house, meowing and trying to get my attention. “What are you doing? Why aren’t you working on that presentation? Why don’t you have time for me?”
It’s funny how we can project our own feelings on others. Of course, the cat didn’t care about the presentation. She only cared about the attention I was giving her while working on it. I’m sure she was happy to have me back. But it’s also true that, sometimes, we work for the cat. We work for the reward, for the money, or for the praise.
There’s nothing wrong with working for the cat. We all do it at times. Just don’t forget to work for yourself. To work on what’s important to you. Because even if you can’t feel it, you are always working for someone.

### Title: Using Your Judgment

### Content: 
In early 1965, Bruce Lee’s father died. He was summoned to Hong Kong to attend the funeral and deal with the estate.
Lee had been in the United States for seven years. He was 24 years old, had a wife and two children, and was just starting to get his career as a martial artist off the ground.
While in Hong Kong, Lee was asked to audition for a role in a TV show. He gave an impressive performance, and the producers offered him the lead role. The show would have been a hit, and Lee would have become a star. But he turned it down and returned to the US.
The reason? “Using his judgment,” his wife Linda wrote in her book Bruce Lee: The Man Only I Knew. “He had to be himself, and it was impossible to be himself in a commercial world.”
It was a decision that would cost him a lot of money, fame, and potentially even his life. But it was the right decision, and Lee would never have forgiven himself for not making it.
Using your judgment is hard. It means saying no when you want to say yes. It means taking the path less traveled. It means leaving money, fame, and comfort behind in order to do the right thing.
But using your judgment is the only way to be yourself. It’s the only way to live a life that’s true to your values. And it’s the only way to find peace and happiness.
So when you’re faced with a difficult decision, remember: using your judgment is always the right thing to do.

### Title: My First Job

### Content: 
That’s an odd phrase to type when you’re 33 years old. But I guess it is. Outside of some internships, only one of which lasted five months instead of just a few weeks, I’ve never held a full-time job—until now. “Business Course Writer.” That’s my title. My responsibility will be to create materials that’ll help enterprise employees understand blockchain and its applications. Kinda cool, huh? I’m definitely not complaining. Storytelling all the way!
I’m not sure I’ll stay in this role for a long time. It’s a contract gig, after all. But I’m excited to see what I can do with it. I’m also excited to have a job, period. It’s a different feeling, isn’t it? Not the best one, but not the worst either. It’s a good feeling to have, and it’s one I’d like to get used to again. I’m not sure I’ll ever be a full-time employee, but I think it’s time to be a part-time one. Let’s see what I can learn from this new experience.
I’m still a writer, still a creator, and I’ll always be an entrepreneur. But I’m also an employee now, and I can’t wait to see what this new hat will teach me.

### Title: Still Water Is a Mirror

### Content: 
“Moving, be like water. Still, be like a mirror.” That’s one of Bruce Lee’s Striking Thoughts. When I read it, I realized that, actually, this is an encouragement to be like water, period.
If you’ve ever seen a lake or pond in complete stillness, you’ll know: Still water is a mirror. It reflects the sky above it, the trees and bushes around it, and everything else that happens to be near it. If you throw a stone into the water, however, it ripples. It moves. It’s no longer a mirror. It’s a participant in what’s going on.
The point of being like water is to know when to move and when to be still. Sometimes, it is enough to observe. To watch. To reflect the world as it is. At other times, however, you must get involved. You must jump in. You must throw a stone into the water.
When you’re still, you can better sense which is which. You can feel whether it is time to act or time to wait. When you’re always moving, you’ll never know. You’ll be too busy to notice anything at all. So be still. Be like a mirror. Until it is time to move, be like water.

### Title: Be Early, or Don’t Be at All

### Content: 
In 2019, I posted every day on Substack for four months straight. My newsletter went from 0 to 4,000 subscribers. It was 100% organic growth with almost zero promotion.
In 2020, I decided to double down. I did a lot of promotion. I guested on podcasts. I wrote guest posts. I went on a Twitter growth spurt. I promoted my newsletter all over the place.
As a result, I got 5,000 new subscribers. It was a 125% increase in subscribers but only a 25% increase in growth. That’s a huge difference.
I learned that if you’re not early, you’re late. In 2019, I was one of the first people to use Substack. I posted every day. I showed up for my audience. I was an early adopter, and I reaped the benefits.
In 2020, I was late. I was no longer an early adopter. I was just another person trying to make it on Substack. And so I had to work a lot harder for the same result.
The same thing happened with Medium. I was an early adopter in 2015. I posted every day for a year. I got a lot of attention and a lot of followers. But then I stopped posting. I was late. And so I had to work a lot harder for the same result.
The lesson here is that if you’re not early, you’re late. And if you’re late, you have to work a lot harder for the same result.
The question is: Are you willing to work a lot harder for the same result? If you are, then go ahead and be late. But if you’re not, then don’t be at all.

### Title: Two Hamsters in the Background

### Content: 
We had some friends over for coffee and cake. Instead of just playing music from a speaker, I put on a lo-fi mix on our TV. Like most music videos of this kind, it featured a drawn wallpaper image. In the background, there were two cute hamsters, sitting, sipping tea from their cups.
As I was talking to my friends, I kept looking at the hamsters. I wondered: “What is their story? Why are they here? Where are they going?” It was as if they were part of our little gathering. I wanted to know more about them. But I never will.
It’s a fascinating aspect of art: You can create a whole new world in a single frame. And even if you only add a little detail to the periphery, the viewer will notice. They might not understand, but they’ll still wonder. “Why is that there? What does it mean?”
The next time you make art, remember: Even the smallest addition can add a big question mark to your creation. Use this power wisely.

### Title: A Good Play To Act Out

### Content: 
In the video game Crisis Core, one of the main characters, Genesis, is obsessed with a poem titled Loveless. Thanks to the developers’ creative efforts, the five-act ballad is a full-fledged piece of art, both in English and Japanese, and it has been featured in Final Fantasy game releases spanning almost 30 years.
In one of the game’s many cutscenes, Genesis recites the first act of the poem to his friend Angeal, who is also one of the protagonists of the story. The two are in a dark cave, and Genesis sits on a rock, reading the poem out loud from a book. As he finishes the last line, Angeal only says: “That’s a good play to act out.”
The line is a bit of an inside joke, as Angeal is referring to the “act” of the poem he just heard. But it’s also a reminder that, yes, life is a play to act out. It’s a story we tell, and while we don’t always get to choose the plot, we can always pick our attitude — and that’s what makes the difference.
Angeal is a soldier, a fighter, and a warrior. He’s not used to reading poetry, but he can appreciate a good story when he hears one. He doesn’t know how his own story will unfold, but he knows he’ll have to fight for what he believes in — and he’s ready to do it.
When life gets tough, remember that you’re not alone. You’re part of a larger story, and there are others who are fighting for the same things you are. Keep your head up, stay strong, and remember that you’re not alone. You’re part of something bigger than yourself, and you have the power to make a difference.
No matter what challenges you face, remember that you have the strength to overcome them. You’re a fighter, and you’re not alone. Keep your head up, stay strong, and never give up on your dreams. You have the power to make a difference, and you’re part of something bigger than yourself.

### Title: Amending Your Words

### Content: 
During his second year at Hogwarts, Dumbledore tells Harry Potter that “help will always be given at Hogwarts to those who ask for it.” And for the next five years, Harry operates under that mantra.
’t ask for help, how can it be given? But in the final installment of the series, Harry learns that the line was never meant to be an absolute. In a moment of crisis, Harry asks Dumbledore’s portrait for advice. The painting says nothing. “But you told me I would always have a way out,” Harry claims. “You told me that help would always be there.”
“I said that help would always be given at Hogwarts to those who ask for it,” Dumbledore corrects him. “But the question was always going to be whether you would ask for it.”
The point is that Dumbledore never said “always” twice. The first time, he was talking about the school. The second time, he was talking about Harry. But in his mind, Harry had merged the two, and it took him a while to realize that the offer of help was only as good as his willingness to accept it.
We do this all the time. We hear something once, and we file it away in our brains forever. That’s fine for some things. The sky is blue, and water is wet. But when it comes to opinions, ideas, and decisions, our minds must stay flexible.
I once told a friend that I thought the word “happiness” was a bad word to use. I argued that it was too vague, too fleeting, and too much of a moving target to be of any use. I suggested “contentment” as a better alternative. My friend disagreed. We debated the matter for a while, but ultimately, he convinced me that I was wrong. I changed my mind. Now, I think happiness is a perfectly fine word to use.
The next time I saw that friend, he brought up the discussion. “Oh yeah, you told me happiness was a bad word.” I reminded him that I had changed my mind. “What do you mean? I thought you were convinced of your argument.” “I was,” I said, “but I’m no longer. I’ve amended my words.”
Amending your words is a good habit. You won’t do it for every sentence you utter, but you should do it for the important ones. The ones that matter. The ones you believe in.
Don’t hold on to your opinions for too long. Keep an open mind. Remember that help will always be given at Hogwarts to those who ask for it. But the question will always be whether you’ll ask for it.

### Title: Remember One Thing

### Content: 
That should be your goal. In each meeting, each conversation. Get one idea to stick in your mind, and you’re golden.
Remember one thing, and you’ll have a good day.
Remember one thing, and you’ll have a good week.
Remember one thing, and you’ll have a good year.
Remember one thing, and you’ll have a good life.
The best way to remember one thing is to remember one thing. Don’t try and capture everything. Don’t take notes. Don’t frantically try to write down every detail. Just be present, and let the most important detail find you.
Then, remember one thing.

### Title: Squeezing Too Early

### Content: 
It’s possible to write a daily blog in 15 minutes. Even ten. Even five. The question is how many minutes went into it before you started typing?
I know people who can write a blog post in five minutes, but it’s only because they’ve been thinking about that post for the last three weeks. They’ve been living it. Living the idea. Then, once it’s ripe, they can sit down and squeeze it out. That’s what we’re doing here. Squeezing ideas.
You can’t squeeze too early. If you do, you’ll only get a few drops. If you wait until the fruit is ripe, however, you’ll get a full glass of juice. Don’t squeeze too early.

### Title: Chocolate for Breakfast

### Content: 
On some days, you’ll need it. Sure, you can sit there, moping, hoping your headache might disappear or that your metabolism will somehow magically kick into gear. Or, you can treat yourself when you need it the most and move on with your day.
A few squares of chocolate for breakfast are not going to make or break your health. They are, however, likely to make or break your mood — and that, too, is worth something.

### Title: Are You Paid Enough To Worry?

### Content: 
My fiancée recently asked me this. I was nervous about a variety of projects going past their deadlines given some reshuffling in our planning at work and me being out sick for a week.
“I’m not sure I’ll be able to get everything done on time. I’m really worried about it.”
“Do you get paid enough to worry about it?”
I thought about it for a moment. I get paid enough to show up and do my best. That’s it. That’s all any job can ask of you.
If you do your best, you can’t fail. You can’t control the outcome, but you can control your effort. The outcome is what you get paid for. The effort is what you control.
The outcome is not worth worrying about. You can’t change it. You can only change your effort. And if you give your best effort, you can be proud of it regardless of the outcome.
The only thing worth worrying about is whether you’re giving your best effort. If you’re not, you can try harder. If you are, there’s no point in worrying.
If you’re not happy with the outcome, you can always get a different job. You can’t control what people think of you, but you can control what you think of yourself. And if you think you’re doing your best, that’s enough.
So, are you paid enough to worry? Probably not. Because worrying is not part of the job. It’s a distraction. A distraction from doing your best. And if you’re not doing your best, you’re not doing your job.
So don’t worry. Just do your best. And be proud of it.

### Title: The Rest Is Confetti

### Content: 
Before she can finally save her siblings from their shared, haunted past that is Hill House, Eleanor “Nell” Crain pays the ultimate price—but it does allow her to send a message, and, sometimes, a message is enough.
The message Nell sends to her brother, Stephen, is simple: “It’s not too late.” It’s not too late to make peace with the dead. It’s not too late to let go of the past. It’s not too late to move on.
It’s never too late for anything, really. There’s always time to change, to make new connections, and to fix what’s broken. We can do all of this at any moment, and yet, it’s hard to believe. The only way to truly grasp this fact is to live it, and that’s why Nell’s message comes with a price: She must die to deliver it.
In a later episode, we see Stephen finally receive the message. It’s a phone call. Nell’s voice on the other end. “It’s not too late,” she says. “It’s not too late for anything.” Stephen is skeptical. “How can you say that? How can you know that?” Nell has an answer: “Because I’m dead.”
In that moment, Stephen realizes: If it’s not too late for the dead, then it’s definitely not too late for the living. The rest is confetti. It’s only a matter of what we choose to believe.
The next time you’re worried about the future, remember Nell’s message: It’s not too late. It’s not too late to make new art. It’s not too late to change your mind. It’s not too late to try a different approach. It’s not too late to have the conversation. It’s not too late to fix what’s broken. It’s not too late to start over. It’s not too late to do it differently. It’s not too late to let go of the past. It’s not too late to move on.
It’s never too late for anything.

### Title: The Humble Shooter

### Content: 
At one point in To Kill a Mockingbird, a dog with rabies slowly walks up to the house of our hero family, the Finches. After housekeeper Calpurnia promptly drags the kids, who discovered the threat, off the street, she calls for their dad, Atticus, to come home.
When Atticus arrives, the sheriff is already there. He asks Atticus to shoot the dog, and after some back and forth, Atticus agrees. He takes the gun, steps out into the street, and with one shot, he kills the dog. The sheriff is impressed, but Atticus doesn’t want to talk about it.
The next day, Atticus’s daughter, Scout, tells her brother Jem about the incident. Jem is proud of their dad, and he tells Scout about Atticus’s past as a great shooter. He explains how Atticus used to be “the deadest shot in Maycomb County,” how he could “shoot a dime out of your hand,” and how he was known as “One-Shot Finch.”
When Scout asks Atticus about it, however, he merely shrugs. “I haven’t shot a gun in years,” he says. “I have no business with a gun. When I was your age I never wanted to be one of those Coffeeville Finches, just a country boy on a farm, like Grandpa.”
Atticus never wanted to be a great shooter. He didn’t enjoy the fame, the attention, or the notoriety that came with it. He only ever used his gift to help others, and as soon as he didn’t need it anymore, he gave it up. It was a tool, nothing more, and he was happy to let it gather dust.
Atticus Finch is a humble man. He doesn’t seek fame. He doesn’t need glory. He just wants to do the right thing, and he’ll do it however he can. That’s why, when the sheriff asks him to shoot the dog, he takes the gun and does what must be done. No more, no less.
When the dog is dead, Atticus hands the gun back to the sheriff and goes about his day. He doesn’t want any credit. He doesn’t need any praise. He’s just happy to have helped, and that’s enough for him.
Atticus Finch is a humble man, and that’s why he’s a great shooter. He doesn’t let his ego get in the way. He doesn’t let his pride cloud his judgment. He just does what needs to be done, and then he moves on.
That’s the kind of shooter we need. The kind of shooter who doesn’t seek the spotlight. The kind of shooter who doesn’t crave attention. The kind of shooter who just wants to do the right thing.
That’s the kind of shooter we need, and that’s the kind of shooter Atticus Finch is. A humble man with a great talent, who uses it only to help others. A man who doesn’t seek fame or glory, but only to do the right thing.
Atticus Finch is a humble man, and that’s why he’s a great shooter. He’s the kind of shooter we need, and that’s why he’s a hero.

### Title: Good People

### Content: 
Those are the ones we seek, aren’t they? But what does “good” mean? Three examples, one lesson.
My dad’s friend is a very good man. He’s a dentist, and when he sees a patient who’s down on their luck, he’ll treat them for free. If they don’t have money for the bus fare, he’ll pay for that too. He’ll even send them home in a taxi if he has to. My dad’s friend does all of this without telling anyone. He doesn’t want credit for it. He just wants to do good.
My friend’s dad is a very good man. He’s a doctor, and when he sees a patient who’s down on their luck, he’ll treat them for free. If they don’t have money for the bus fare, he’ll pay for that too. He’ll even send them home in a taxi if he has to. My friend’s dad does all of this without telling anyone. He doesn’t want credit for it. He just wants to do good.
My neighbor is a very good man. He’s a baker, and when he sees a customer who’s down on their luck, he’ll give them a free pretzel. If they don’t have money for the bus fare, he’ll pay for that too. He’ll even send them home in a taxi if he has to. My neighbor does all of this without telling anyone. He doesn’t want credit for it. He just wants to do good.
What’s the lesson? The lesson is that good people are all around us. We just have to look. Don’t be so busy. Don’t be so distracted. Look for the good people. They’re everywhere.

### Title: Skipping Politics

### Content: 
I rarely comment on politics, the economy, or global affairs on this blog. It’s not for a lack of opinions.
I have plenty of opinions, but I’ve learned that sharing them is rarely productive. For one, I’m not an expert on any of these topics. I don’t have the time to be an expert on any of these topics. I can’t even be an expert on all of the topics I care about. Therefore, I can’t offer much more than a layman’s opinion — and that’s not worth much.
I can’t add to the conversation. I can only add noise. And I don’t want to be part of the noise. I want to be part of the solution. That’s why I write about productivity, habits, and self-improvement. It’s what I know. It’s what I’m good at. It’s where I can make a difference.
It’s hard to resist the temptation of spouting your opinion on the latest news, but it’s rarely worth the satisfaction. Unless you can be part of the solution, it’s better to stay silent — and if you can’t be part of the solution, you can always work on something else where you can.

### Title: The Worst Pain Is Fear

### Content: 
The dentist is a great place to practice. Patience. Courage. Trust. But most of all: avoiding needless suffering.
When you’re sitting in the dentist’s chair, there are many ways to make the experience more painful than it already is. You can clench your teeth, tighten your muscles, and hold your breath. You can imagine the worst possible outcomes. You can dwell on the pain that’s already there. You can try to mentally escape the situation, and you can try to control it.
All of these are distractions. They only make the situation worse. The pain is already there. You can’t change that. The only question is will you add to it? Will you pile on more suffering? Or will you accept the pain that’s already there?
The best thing you can do in the dentist’s chair is to let go. Relax. Surrender. Breathe. Trust the process. Have faith that, soon, it will all be over. That’s the only way to not make the pain worse.
Life is like sitting in the dentist’s chair. It’s not always comfortable. Sometimes, it hurts. But the worst pain is fear. The fear of the pain that’s about to come. The fear of the pain that might come. The fear of the pain that’s already there.
The best thing we can do is to not add to that fear. To accept the pain that’s already there. To sit with it. Make room for it. Breathe. And trust the process.
Soon, it will all be over.

### Title: What Do You Not Want To Do Today?

### Content: 
We were sipping on preposterous, eight-euro tea in the Four Seasons lobby when my friend Michael walked me through his daily journaling prompts.
The first one? “What do you not want to do today?”
I thought it was brilliant. How many times have I gone to bed thinking, “I wish I hadn’t done that today?” A lot. But how often did I ask myself that question in advance? Never.
It’s a simple question, but it can lead to powerful answers. It’s also a question we rarely ask. We’re so busy trying to figure out what we want to do that we forget to consider what we don’t want to do.
The point of the question is not to make you feel bad for what you didn’t do. It’s to make you feel good for what you didn’t do.
If you don’t want to do something, don’t do it. That’s the whole point. You can either avoid it altogether or do it later. The important thing is to acknowledge it and make a conscious decision.
It’s okay to not want to do something. It’s okay to not want to do something that’s important. It’s okay to not want to do something that’s urgent. It’s okay to not want to do something that’s good for you.
The only thing that’s not okay is to not want to do something and then do it anyway. That’s how you end up feeling bad for what you didn’t do.
So ask yourself: What do you not want to do today? And then don’t do it.

### Title: Remembering This

### Content: 
In 2014, I was an intern at BMW M in Munich. I lived in a tiny apartment offered by the company that somehow still cost almost my entire below-minimum-wage salary. I was young, relatively broke, and single.
One night, I went out with some friends. We went to a fancy club. I didn’t have much money, so I only drank one or two beers. I also didn’t have a lot of experience in clubs, so I mostly stood around and observed.
At some point, I noticed a guy who was also alone. He had a drink in his hand, and he was just standing there, looking around. He didn’t seem to be having a good time. I thought: “Wow. This guy has no idea what he’s doing. He’s totally lost.”
But then, as I looked at him more closely, I realized: “Wait a minute. That’s me. I’m looking at myself in a mirror.” I had no idea how long I had been staring at my own reflection, but it was long enough to make some pretty harsh judgments about myself.
I laughed and decided to leave the club. I walked home alone, and on the way, I had a lot of time to think. I realized that, sometimes, it’s easy to forget that we’re all in the same boat. We’re all struggling with something, and we all have our own challenges to face.
It’s easy to look at someone and think, “Wow, that person has no idea what they’re doing.” But the truth is, we’re all just trying our best. We’re all lost sometimes. We all have moments when we feel like we’re not good enough, or that we don’t belong.
But the important thing is to remember that we’re not alone. We’re all in this together, and we all have the power to help each other. We can offer a kind word, a helping hand, or just a smile to someone who needs it.
So, the next time you find yourself judging someone, remember: you’re looking at yourself in a mirror. We’re all lost sometimes, but we’re all in this together. Let’s help each other find our way.
